DV-PRTY-036.question: Labor vote Special Minister of State - Stop 2015?
DV-PRTY-036.answer:
On 3 December 2015 the House of Representatives passed the motion on the Special Minister of State.

Bill Shorten sought leave to move that the House had no confidence in the Special Minister of State and Minister for Defence Materiel and Science, saying parliament must act if the Prime Minister would not.

Mark Dreyfus seconded the censure motion, telling the House the minister had misled it five times, including twice in the preceding hour.

Tony Burke called it the last chance for someone to defend the minister.

- Bill Shorten sought leave to move that the House had no confidence in the Special Minister of State and Minister for Defence Materiel and Science, saying the parliament must act if the Prime Minister would not.

- Tony Burke pressed the crossbench and government benches by calling it the last chance for someone to defend the minister.

TT-YDEB-004.question: Who were the most prominent voices in the the Canberra bushfires debate in 2003?
TT-YDEB-004.answer:
Nick Minchin, answering a question on notice on 24 November 2003, detailed Treasury interest-free loans to employees affected by the 18 January 2003 fires.

- Annette Ellis described how the 18 January 2003 fires struck her own community while she was at home in Monash, a suburb of Tuggeranong, in a 5 February 2003 speech.

- Stewart McArthur, speaking on 5 November 2003 after the bushfire inquiry hearings in Canberra and Cooma, focused on fuel reduction and criticised state authorities and the green movement for silence on the fires.
- Kate Lundy in an adjournment speech the day before, on 4 February 2003.

sources.title: Annette Ellis — 2003-02-05
sources.snippet: In beginning my contribution today, could I make the point that, whilst I am obviously going to be concentrating on the fires in Canberra of 18 January, I fully recognise and acknowledge that there have been severe fires in Queensland, Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania and Western Australia—in fact, virtually right across the continent. Saturday, 18 January 2003 was a devastating day for Canberra. Fires—begun by a lightning strike some time earlier and encouraged and fed by terrain, weather conditions and extreme drought—hit our community in a way never imagined. I was at home that day in Monash, a suburb of Tuggeranong, and my neighbours and I heard the emergency warnings and prepared our houses. At the time, we had no way of knowing the actual dimension of what was happening, except to say that the heat, the wind and the overwhelming red glow followed by darkness—virtually as dark as midnight—in the middle of the afternoon told us something terrible was happening. We were lucky because the fires did not actually reach our suburb. But the statistics I am referring to are stark. It is worth noting, in referring to those statistics, that up until this time I believe it had been 51
sources.speaker: Annette Ellis

sources.title: Richard Kenneth Robert Alston — HIGHER EDUCATION LEGISLATION AMENDMENT BILL 2003 — 2003-08-13
sources.snippet: The bill provides $7.3 million in 2003 to assist the Australian National University rebuild its world class research facilities at Mt Stromlo Observatory following their devastation by the Canberra bushfires on 18 January 2003. The bushfires that swept through the Research School of Astronomy and Astrophysics site destroyed heritage buildings, critical workshops and state-of-the-art telescopes that were also a key tourist attraction. The Research School has long been recognised as an important player in national and international astronomy, providing leading edge training for students as well as world class pure and applied research facilities.
sources.speaker: Richard Kenneth Robert Alston

sources.title: Nick Minchin — QUESTIONS ON NOTICE — 2003-11-24
sources.snippet: (2) Following the bushfires that struck Canberra on 18 January 2003, the Treasury made an offer of assistance to employees who were directly affected by the fires - that is, through loss or substantial damage to their homes. The offer included short-term, interest free loans, based on demonstrated need. Two employees took up the offer. They were loaned $2000 and $1000 respectively. The latter has been repaid in full; the former is subject to regular repayments and will be fully paid in November.
sources.speaker: Nick Minchin

sources.title: Stewart McArthur — 2003-11-05
sources.snippet: A nation charred is the result of 500 submissions from those people at the coalface of firefighting—firefighters, landowners, farmers and community people—who have been personally affected by the fires. The impact of this devastation is evidenced by the hearings that were held in Omeo, Buchan, Wodonga, Canberra and Cooma, so much so that those of us who attended those hearings were on the verge of crying when we heard about the devastation that was brought about by these fires. The fact of the matter is that four million hectares were burnt; nothing can refute that fundamental evidence. The fires burnt out about 56 years of forest production in current harvesting rates and the fires were so hot that it will mean that much of it will not recover. National parks were devastated and there is very strong evidence that this was the worst fire since 1939.The observation I make is that there was a conspiracy of silence by state authorities, bushfire brigades and the green movement, who made no comment on the fires. They were strangely silent. They said nothing for weeks and weeks about this absolute devastation. There was overwhelming evidence that fuel reduction burning is a desirable te
sources.speaker: Stewart McArthur

sources.title: Kate Lundy — ADJOURNMENT — 2003-02-04
sources.snippet: A bushfire recovery appeal has been set up and is receiving strong local and outside support, with many businesses and organisations donating quite extraordinary amounts of money. About $3½ million has been collected to date. From memory, the target was $10 million for this fund. I would like to mention some of the donors to that fund. Licensed clubs throughout Canberra have rallied to the emergency by not only donating large amounts of money to the bushfire recovery appeal through ClubsACT but providing food and facilities and supporting emergency services and the efforts of other organisations. In some cases, this was as straightforward as making sandwiches on the day. In the week following the firestorm— when Belconnen and other places were still on alert; we had no idea if the fires were going to come back—those clubs made sandwiches to make sure that the volunteers, the firies and the emergency services workers had food to be able to keep going. Those little things really mattered and made a big difference.
sources.speaker: Kate Lundy
